summary: Extends RSVP-TE to bind two point-to-point unidirectional label switched paths into one associated bidirectional path. It defines new Association Types for the ASSOCIATION and Extended ASSOCIATION objects, supporting two-way traffic where each direction may follow a different route.

eli5.summary: Two one-way streets that together act like a two-way road. This gives them a shared label so the network knows they belong to the same trip.

questions: what is an associated bidirectional lsp
what is single-sided provisioning in rsvp-te
subtitle: How RSVP-TE ties two one-way label switched paths into a single two-way path, with independent or one-sided setup.

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile requires associated bidirectional point-to-point LSPs, but RSVP-TE had no way to say that two opposite one-way LSPs belong together.
tldr.mechanism: Two new Association Types (3 and 4) for the ASSOCIATION and Extended ASSOCIATION objects bind the two LSPs, and a new REVERSE_LSP object lets one endpoint trigger and shape the reverse LSP.
tldr.outcome: Each direction can take a different route and have different bandwidth. RFC 7551 is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 8537 updates it.

today: RFC 7551 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2015, and it is updated by RFC 8537. The RFC text does not describe any deployments.

sections.title: The Need for Associated Bidirectional LSPs
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile requirements (RFC 5654) say MPLS-TP MUST support associated bidirectional point-to-point LSPs, that the end points MUST be aware of the pairing, and that bidirectional LSPs with asymmetric bandwidth MUST be supported. Such paths are also useful for OAM messages that need a return path.

The ASSOCIATION object already existed (RFC 4872), mainly to link a recovery LSP to the LSP it protects, and RFC 6780 added the Extended ASSOCIATION object. RFC 7551 defines two new Association Types for these objects, plus a REVERSE_LSP object.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you need a road in both directions, but the two directions do not have to be the same road. This lets the network pair two one-way roads and treat them as a team.

sections.title: Two Provisioning Models
sections.content:
An associated bidirectional LSP is made of two reverse unidirectional LSPs. Each one starts where the other ends. They are still established, monitored and protected independently, and the forward and reverse paths may take different routes. The RFC's example has LSP1 going A, D, B and LSP2 going B, D, C, A.

There are two ways to set them up:

  • Single-sided provisioning: the tunnel is configured on one endpoint only. That endpoint sends a Path message with an (Extended) ASSOCIATION object and a REVERSE_LSP object, and the other endpoint creates and signals the reverse LSP in response.
  • Double-sided provisioning: two unidirectional tunnels are configured independently, one at each endpoint, and both are signaled with (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects.

In both cases the LSPs are bound by identical (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects in their Path messages. For asymmetric bandwidth in the single-sided case, a SENDER_TSPEC subobject inside the REVERSE_LSP object sets the reverse bandwidth. In the double-sided case the two LSPs are set up with separate bandwidths, which may or may not be identical.
sections.eli5: Either one person sets up both roads and tells the other end "build the way back like this," or each end builds its own road and both stamp it with the same tag.

sections.title: The New Association Types and REVERSE_LSP Object
sections.content:
The new Association Types are value 3 for Double-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP and value 4 for Single-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP. The Association ID and Association Source MUST be set by the node that originates the association. In the Extended object, the Global Association Source is the Global_ID of that node.

The REVERSE_LSP object (Class_Num 203, C_Type 1) is carried in the Path message of the forward LSP. It holds zero or more subobjects that have the same format as RSVP objects and override the default contents of the reverse LSP's Path message. Any object that may be carried in a Path message MAY be carried inside it. Examples include SENDER_TSPEC, EXPLICIT_ROUTE, SESSION_ATTRIBUTE, ADMIN_STATUS, LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES and PROTECTION.
sections.eli5: There are two new tag colours, one for "both ends set this up" and one for "one end set this up." There is also a note that the first end can attach to say how the way back should be built.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
An ingress node MUST insert an (Extended) ASSOCIATION object into the Path message and set the Association Type to the single-sided or double-sided value. Single-sided and double-sided types MUST NOT appear in the same Path message. These types apply only in Path messages and SHOULD NOT be used in Resv messages. Association is identified by the rules in RFC 6780: the objects must be identical.

For single-sided provisioning the Path message MUST carry the REVERSE_LSP object. The egress node MUST verify that a matching single-sided association is present. If not, it MUST NOT trigger a reverse LSP. Otherwise it MUST create the reverse LSP or reject the Path message, and on failure it returns a PathErr with Error Code "Admission Control Failure" (1) and the new Sub-code "Reverse LSP Failure" (6).

Anything missing from the REVERSE_LSP object is filled in from the forward Path message: the egress node SHOULD copy SESSION_ATTRIBUTE, CLASS_TYPE, LABEL_REQUEST, ASSOCIATION, ADMIN_STATUS and PROTECTION, and it swaps the SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE addresses. Changes to the forward LSP MUST result in matching changes in the reverse LSP. If the forward LSP is torn down, the egress node MUST remove the reverse LSP. If only the reverse LSP is torn down, the initiating LSP is not removed.
sections.eli5: The far end checks the tag, builds the way back using the notes it was given, and copies anything the notes left out. If it cannot build the road, it sends back an error.

sections.title: Compatibility and Recovery
sections.content:
The ASSOCIATION, Extended ASSOCIATION and REVERSE_LSP objects all have class numbers of the form 11bbbbbb, so nodes that do not understand them ignore the object but forward it unchanged. Operators SHOULD make sure every node expected to act on an association supports the type. An egress node that does not support the new types is expected to return a PathErr with Error Code "Admission Control Failure" (1) and Sub-code "Bad Association Type" (5).

Recovery of each direction is independent. LSP recovery from RFC 4872 and RFC 4873 is not affected, because it uses a different Association Type, and several ASSOCIATION objects can appear in one Path message.
sections.eli5: Old routers that do not know the new tags just pass them along without reading them, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA registered Association Types 3 and 4 in the Association Type subregistry, Class Number 203 (C-Type 1) for REVERSE_LSP, and the "Reverse LSP Failure" sub-code 6 under Error Code 1.

On security, the new Association Types by themselves add no information to signaling, and the related considerations are covered in RFC 6780. The REVERSE_LSP object can carry parameters for the reverse LSP, but this is not fundamentally different from information already carried for a bidirectional LSP, and processing remains subject to local policy. For general MPLS and GMPLS security, the RFC points to RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: The new tags add no big new risks beyond the ones these networks already handle, and the usual security rules still apply.
